questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 88 · Registers of members and security holders
questions.stem: Under section 88(1) of the Companies Act 2013, from what point must a company keep and maintain the register of members, the register of debenture-holders and the register of any other security holders?

readLink.label: Read: Registers of members and security holders — ss. 88, 94 and 95 →

options.text: From the date of its registration
options.explanation: Correct. Section 88(1) requires the registers to be kept and maintained 'from the date of its registration', in the prescribed form, the register of members being kept separately for each class of equity and preference shares.

options.text: From the date of the first annual general meeting
options.explanation: The obligation does not wait for a meeting. It attaches on registration, long before the first AGM.

options.text: From the date on which the company first allots shares to the public
options.explanation: Section 88 applies to every company, including one that never approaches the public. Allotment is not the trigger.

options.text: From the date of the declaration for commencement of business under section 10A
options.explanation: Section 10A governs the commencement of business and borrowing. It has nothing to do with the register obligation, which starts on registration.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 88(3)–(4) · Depository register and foreign register
questions.stem: Kaveri Exports Limited wishes to keep, in Singapore, a part of its register of members containing the particulars of its members resident in Singapore. Which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Registers of members and security holders — ss. 88, 94 and 95 →

options.text: It may do so only with the previous approval of the Central Government, and the foreign register is a register independent of the principal register
options.explanation: No Central Government approval is required, and the foreign register is expressly deemed to be part of the principal register, not independent of it.

options.text: It may do so if its articles so authorise, and the foreign register is deemed to be part of the company's principal register
options.explanation: Correct. Section 88(4) permits a company 'if so authorised by its articles' to keep in any country outside India a part of the register of members, debenture-holders or other security holders resident in that country, and calls it a foreign register, which is deemed to be part of the principal register.

options.text: It may do so only after a special resolution passed at a general meeting, because the register is being moved out of the registered office
options.explanation: The special resolution requirement belongs to section 94(1), which governs keeping the registers at another place IN INDIA. A foreign register runs on the authority of the articles.

options.text: It may not do so at all, because section 94 requires every register under section 88 to be kept at the registered office in India
options.explanation: Section 94 opens with the words 'save as otherwise provided', and section 88(4) is that other provision. A foreign register is lawful.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 89 · Declaration of beneficial interest
questions.stem: Shares of Bhagirathi Chemicals Limited stand registered in the name of Mr Prabhu, but the entire beneficial interest in them belongs to Ms Sundari. Under section 89, who must make a declaration to the company?

readLink.label: Read: Beneficial interest and significant beneficial owners — ss. 89 and 90 →

options.text: Ms Sundari alone, since she alone holds the beneficial interest
options.explanation: Section 89(2) does require her declaration, but section 89(1) independently requires the registered holder to declare that he does not hold the beneficial interest. Both must file.

options.text: Mr Prabhu alone, since only the person on the register is known to the company
options.explanation: Section 89(2) fastens on the beneficial owner precisely because the company does not know him. Both declarations are due.

options.text: Neither, so long as the company is informed of the arrangement by its registrar and transfer agent
options.explanation: Section 89 prescribes declarations by named persons in the prescribed form. Information from an intermediary is not a substitute.

options.text: Both Mr Prabhu, under section 89(1), and Ms Sundari, under section 89(2), each within thirty days
options.explanation: Correct. The registered holder who does not hold the beneficial interest declares under s. 89(1); the person holding the beneficial interest but not registered declares under s. 89(2); each has thirty days, and the company then files its own return under s. 89(6).

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 89(2) · The thirty-day declaration clock
questions.stem: Ms Sundari acquires the beneficial interest in 20,000 shares of Bhagirathi Chemicals Limited on 12 May 2026, the shares remaining registered in the name of Mr Prabhu. The last date by which she must make her declaration to the company under section 89(2) is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 89(2) — thirty days from the date of acquiring the beneficial interest

readLink.label: Read: Beneficial interest and significant beneficial owners — ss. 89 and 90 →

options.explanation: Fifteen days is not a period known to section 89, and fifteen days from 12 May 2026 is 27 May. Every clock in the section is thirty days.

options.text: 11 June 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days counted from (and excluding) 12 May 2026: nineteen days remain in May, and the thirtieth day falls on 11 June 2026.

options.text: 12 June 2026
options.explanation: This reads the period as one calendar month rather than thirty days, and lands one day late. May has thirty-one days, so thirty days from 12 May is 11 June.

options.text: 10 August 2026
options.explanation: Ninety days appears nowhere in section 89. It is a distractor drawn from other chapters.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 90 · Significant beneficial owner
questions.stem: Which statement about the significant beneficial owner under section 90 of the Companies Act 2013 is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 90(1) read with the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules 2018

readLink.label: Read: Beneficial interest and significant beneficial owners — ss. 89 and 90 →

options.text: Any person, whether an individual or a body corporate, holding not less than ten per cent of the shares of a company is a significant beneficial owner
options.explanation: Section 90 reaches only INDIVIDUALS. The whole purpose of the section is to look through bodies corporate and trusts to the natural person behind them.

options.text: Only an individual who is a resident of India can be a significant beneficial owner
options.explanation: Section 90(1) expressly contemplates holdings through one or more persons or trusts, 'including a trust and persons resident outside India'. Residence is not the test.

options.text: An individual who, acting alone or together or through one or more persons or a trust, holds beneficial interests of not less than twenty-five per cent, or such other percentage as may be prescribed, or has the right to exercise significant influence or control, is a significant beneficial owner
options.explanation: Correct. That is the structure of section 90(1): an individual, the twenty-five per cent figure subject to a prescribed alternative (presently ten per cent under the SBO Rules), and the independent limb of significant influence or control.

options.text: The declaration is made by the company to the significant beneficial owner, who must then acknowledge it within thirty days
options.explanation: The direction of the declaration is reversed. The individual declares to the company; the company maintains a register and files a return with the Registrar.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 90(5)–(9) · Enforcement against a significant beneficial owner
questions.stem: A company gives notice to a person it has reason to believe is a significant beneficial owner. The person does not reply. Under section 90, what is the company's next step, and before whom?

readLink.label: Read: Beneficial interest and significant beneficial owners — ss. 89 and 90 →

options.text: Apply to the Tribunal within fifteen days of the expiry of the thirty-day reply period, for an order restricting the rights attached to the shares
options.explanation: Correct. Section 90(7) requires the company to apply to the Tribunal within fifteen days of the expiry of the period allowed for the reply, for an order directing restrictions on transfer of interest, suspension of voting rights, suspension of the right to receive dividend, or other restrictions.

options.text: Apply to the Registrar of Companies, who may direct the transfer of the shares to the Investor Education and Protection Fund
options.explanation: The Registrar has no such power. The application lies to the Tribunal, and transfer to the IEPF is a consequence only where no relaxation application is made within one year of the Tribunal's order.

options.text: Apply to the Central Government within thirty days for permission to cancel the shares
options.explanation: Neither the forum nor the remedy is right. Section 90 nowhere allows cancellation of shares, and the Central Government is not the authority.

options.text: Do nothing further, because the obligation to declare rests on the individual and the company has discharged its duty by giving notice
options.explanation: Section 90(7) makes the application mandatory once the person fails to give the information or the company is not satisfied with the reply. Inaction is itself a default.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 91 · Closure of the register
questions.stem: Under section 91 of the Companies Act 2013, a company may close its register of members:

readLink.label: Read: Closure of the register — s. 91 →

options.text: For any period or periods not exceeding thirty days in the aggregate in each year, and not exceeding fifteen days at any one time
options.explanation: The two figures are transposed and understated. The aggregate is forty-five days a year and the single-spell ceiling is thirty days.

options.text: For a single continuous period not exceeding forty-five days in each year
options.explanation: Forty-five days is the annual aggregate across all spells, not a permissible single spell. No single spell may exceed thirty days.

options.text: For any period or periods not exceeding forty-five days in the aggregate in each year, but not exceeding thirty days at any one time, after previous notice of at least seven days in the prescribed manner
options.explanation: Correct. Section 91(1) imposes both ceilings simultaneously and requires previous notice of at least seven days, or such lesser period as SEBI may specify for a listed company or a company intending to list.

options.text: For any period it thinks fit, provided a special resolution is passed and notice is filed with the Registrar
options.explanation: Section 91 needs no resolution at all. It needs previous public notice and compliance with the two statutory ceilings.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 94 · Place of keeping registers
questions.stem: Yamuna Foods Limited, with its registered office at Indore, wants to keep its register of members and copies of its annual returns at Bhopal, where 1,900 of its 12,000 members reside. What does section 94(1) require?

readLink.label: Read: Registers of members and security holders — ss. 88, 94 and 95 →

options.text: Nothing more than a Board resolution, since the registers are only being moved within the same State
options.explanation: The State makes no difference to section 94, and a Board resolution is not enough. A special resolution of the members is required.

options.text: A special resolution passed at a general meeting, the condition as to residence being satisfied because more than one-tenth of the members reside at Bhopal
options.explanation: Correct. 1,900 exceeds one-tenth of 12,000, which is 1,200, so the residence condition is met; section 94(1) then requires approval by a special resolution passed at a general meeting.

options.text: A special resolution and, in addition, the previous approval of the Regional Director
options.explanation: No Regional Director approval is involved. That approver belongs to the registered-office provisions of section 12, not to section 94.

options.text: An ordinary resolution, together with the consent of members holding more than one-tenth of the paid-up share capital
options.explanation: Two errors. The resolution must be special, and the one-tenth test is measured on the NUMBER OF MEMBERS residing at the place, not on capital.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 94 and 95 · Inspection and evidentiary value
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the registers maintained under sections 88 and 94 is INCORRECT?

readLink.label: Read: Registers of members and security holders — ss. 88, 94 and 95 →

options.text: A member, debenture-holder, other security holder or beneficial owner may inspect them during business hours without payment of any fee
options.explanation: This is correct law under section 94(2); free inspection for these persons, and inspection on payment of the prescribed fee for anyone else.

options.text: The articles may impose reasonable restrictions on inspection, but not less than two hours on every business day must be allowed
options.explanation: This is correct law. The two-hour floor in section 94(2) survives any restriction the articles impose.

options.text: A person requiring a copy of the register must be furnished with it within seven days of his request
options.explanation: This is correct law under section 94(3), and refusal or delay attracts a per-day penalty under section 94(4).

options.text: The registers and the copies of annual returns are conclusive evidence of the matters entered in them and cannot be contradicted
options.explanation: Correct — this is the incorrect statement, and therefore the answer. Section 95 makes them PRIMA FACIE evidence of any matter directed or authorised to be inserted by the Act, which means the entries are rebuttable by better evidence.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 92(1) · Contents of the annual return
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT among the contents of the annual return prescribed by section 92(1) as it presently stands?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 92(1) — clauses (c) and (j) omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2017

readLink.label: Read: Annual return — s. 92 →

options.text: Particulars of the company's holding, subsidiary and associate companies
options.explanation: This is expressly required, alongside the registered office and the principal business activities.

options.text: The indebtedness of the company
options.explanation: Correct. The clause requiring the company's indebtedness was OMITTED by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2017, along with the clause on shares held by or on behalf of foreign institutional investors. Both are classic distractors.

options.text: Meetings of members or a class of members, of the Board and of its committees, along with attendance details
options.explanation: This is required. The return records the meeting record of the company for the year.

options.text: Penalties imposed on the company, its directors or officers, and details of compounding of offences and appeals made against such penalties
options.explanation: This is required, and is one of the more heavily examined clauses.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 92(1) provisos · Signing the annual return
questions.stem: Sahyadri Tools Private Limited is a small company and has no company secretary. Its annual return must be signed by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 92(1), first and third provisos

readLink.label: Read: Annual return — s. 92 →

options.text: A company secretary in practice, because the company has no company secretary of its own
options.explanation: That is the general rule for companies other than an OPC or a small company. For a small company the Act supplies a lighter alternative.

options.text: A director of the company
options.explanation: Correct. For a One Person Company and a small company the annual return is signed by the company secretary, or, where there is no company secretary, by the DIRECTOR of the company. No practising professional need sign.

options.text: A director and the statutory auditor of the company
options.explanation: The auditor never signs the annual return. He reports on the financial statements, a separate document.

options.text: Two directors, one of whom must be a managing director where the company has one
options.explanation: That signing formula belongs to the financial statements under section 134, not to the annual return.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 92 · Certification of the annual return in MGT-8
questions.stem: Which of these unlisted companies must have its annual return certified by a company secretary in practice under the second proviso to section 92(1)?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 92(1), second proviso, read with rule 11(2) of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules 2014 — thresholds are rules-level

readLink.label: Read: Annual return — s. 92 →

options.text: A company with paid-up share capital of ₹6 crore and turnover of ₹38 crore
options.explanation: Both limbs fail: ₹6 crore is below the ₹10 crore paid-up threshold and ₹38 crore is below the ₹50 crore turnover threshold. No certification is required.

options.text: A company with paid-up share capital of ₹9.50 crore and turnover of ₹44 crore
options.explanation: Again both limbs fail, and by design: the figures sit just under each threshold to test whether you check both.

options.text: A company with paid-up share capital of ₹4 crore and turnover of ₹62 crore
options.explanation: Correct. The two limbs are joined by OR, so one is enough. Turnover of ₹62 crore is at or above ₹50 crore, and certification in Form MGT-8 is required even though the paid-up capital is well below ₹10 crore.

options.text: A company with paid-up share capital of ₹9 crore and turnover of ₹49 crore, because the two figures together exceed ₹50 crore
options.explanation: The limbs are alternatives, not addends. Paid-up capital and turnover are never added together for this test.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 92(4) · Filing the annual return
questions.stem: Ravikiran Textiles Limited, whose financial year closed on 31 March 2026, held its annual general meeting on 18 September 2026. The last date for filing its annual return with the Registrar under section 92(4) is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 92(4) — sixty days from the date on which the AGM is held

readLink.label: Read: Annual return — s. 92 →

options.explanation: This counts sixty days from the close of the financial year. Section 92(4) runs from the AGM, not from the year-end.

options.text: 18 October 2026
options.explanation: This allows only thirty days. Thirty days is the section 117 and section 121 clock; the annual return has sixty.

options.text: 29 November 2026
options.explanation: This counts sixty days from 30 September 2026, the last date on which the AGM SHOULD have been held. That start point applies only where no AGM was in fact held.

options.text: 17 November 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Sixty days counted from (and excluding) 18 September 2026: twelve days to 30 September, thirty-one more to 31 October, and seventeen more to 17 November 2026.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 96 · The first annual general meeting
questions.stem: Sanchay Instruments Private Limited was incorporated on 5 August 2025. Its first financial year closed on 31 March 2026. The last date by which it must hold its first annual general meeting is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 96(1), first proviso — nine months from the date of closing of the first financial year

readLink.label: Read: Annual general meeting — s. 96 →

options.text: 31 December 2026
options.explanation: Correct. The first annual general meeting must be held within nine months from the date of closing of the FIRST FINANCIAL YEAR: nine months from 31 March 2026 is 31 December 2026. The company also need hold no AGM in its year of incorporation.

options.text: 30 September 2026
options.explanation: Six months from the close of the financial year is the rule for every AGM EXCEPT the first. The first gets nine months.
This counts nine months from the date of INCORPORATION. The proviso runs from the closing of the first financial year, not from incorporation.

options.text: 31 March 2027
options.explanation: Twelve months from the year-end is not a period known to section 96, and it would in any event breach the fifteen-month gap discipline in later years.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 96 · Subsequent AGM and the fifteen-month gap
questions.stem: Meghdoot Cables Limited closed its financial year on 31 March 2026. Its previous annual general meeting was held on 2 May 2025. Ignoring any extension by the Registrar, the last date by which it must hold its next annual general meeting is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 96(1) — six months from the close of the financial year, and a gap of not more than fifteen months between AGMs

readLink.label: Read: Annual general meeting — s. 96 →

options.text: 30 September 2026
options.explanation: This applies only the six-month rule and ignores the fifteen-month gap, which expires earlier and therefore governs.

options.text: 2 November 2026
options.explanation: Eighteen months from the previous AGM. Section 96(1) caps the gap at fifteen months, not eighteen.

options.text: 2 August 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Two limits apply at once: six months from 31 March 2026 gives 30 September 2026, and fifteen months from 2 May 2025 gives 2 August 2026. The EARLIER date governs, so the AGM must be held by 2 August 2026.

options.text: 31 December 2026
options.explanation: Nine months from the year-end is the first-AGM period. This is not a first AGM.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 96(1), third proviso · Extension of time by the Registrar
questions.stem: Regarding the extension of time for holding an annual general meeting, which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Annual general meeting — s. 96 →

options.text: The Tribunal may, for any special reason, extend the time for holding any annual general meeting, including the first, by up to three months
options.explanation: The authority is wrong. The extension is granted by the REGISTRAR, and the Tribunal's role under section 97 arises only after a default.

options.text: The Registrar may extend the time for holding any annual general meeting, including the first, by up to six months
options.explanation: Both the exclusion and the period are wrong. The maximum extension is three months, and the first AGM cannot be extended at all.

options.text: The Registrar may, for any special reason, extend the time within which any annual general meeting other than the first shall be held, by a period not exceeding three months
options.explanation: Correct. That is the third proviso to section 96(1) word for word in substance: a special reason, the Registrar as the authority, a maximum of three months, and the express exclusion of the first AGM.

options.text: The Central Government may extend the time by up to three months, and the extension is available for the first annual general meeting as well
options.explanation: The Central Government has no such power here, and the first AGM is expressly outside the extension.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 96(2) · Time and place of the AGM
questions.stem: Which statement about the time and place of an annual general meeting under section 96(2) is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 96(2) and its first proviso and Explanation

readLink.label: Read: Annual general meeting — s. 96 →

options.text: It must be called during business hours, that is between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m., on a day that is not a National Holiday, and held at the registered office or some other place within the city, town or village in which the registered office is situate; an unlisted company may hold it at any place in India with the advance consent of all its members
options.explanation: Correct. That is section 96(2) with its first proviso. Note that the relaxation as to place is available to UNLISTED companies only and needs the consent of ALL members, given in writing or in electronic mode in advance.

options.text: It may be held on any day and at any hour, provided the notice states the day and hour and no member objects
options.explanation: Section 96(2) fixes both the hours and the class of day. Absence of objection cures nothing.

options.text: It must not be held on a Sunday or on any public holiday declared by the State Government
options.explanation: The bar is on a NATIONAL HOLIDAY, which the Explanation defines as a day declared as such by the Central Government. A Sunday or a State holiday is not barred.

options.text: A listed company may hold its annual general meeting at any place in India if the members holding ninety-five per cent of the paid-up capital consent in advance
options.explanation: Two errors. The relaxation applies to unlisted companies, and it needs the consent of all members, not a ninety-five per cent block.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 97 · Tribunal's power to call a defaulted AGM
questions.stem: Panchganga Alloys Limited has failed to hold its annual general meeting within the time allowed by section 96. Which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Tribunal-called meetings and default — ss. 97, 98 and 99 →

options.text: Only the Registrar may now direct the company to hold the meeting, and only after issuing a show-cause notice
options.explanation: The Registrar's role under section 96 is to extend time in advance, not to call a meeting after default. Section 97 places the power in the Tribunal.

options.text: The Central Government may, on a complaint by any creditor, direct the company to hold the meeting
options.explanation: No such power exists, and a creditor is not the person section 97 empowers to move.

options.text: The Tribunal may call the meeting only on the application of members holding not less than one-tenth of the paid-up voting capital
options.explanation: That one-tenth threshold belongs to a requisitioned extraordinary general meeting under section 100(2). Section 97 may be moved by ANY member.

options.text: The Tribunal may, on the application of any member, call or direct the calling of an annual general meeting and give ancillary directions, including a direction that one member present in person or by proxy shall be deemed to constitute a meeting
options.explanation: Correct. Section 97(1) allows any member to apply; the Tribunal acts notwithstanding anything in the Act or the articles, and the one-member direction is expressly available. The meeting so held is deemed to be an annual general meeting.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 98 and 99 · Impracticable meetings and punishment
questions.stem: Which statement about section 98 of the Companies Act 2013 is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Tribunal-called meetings and default — ss. 97, 98 and 99 →

options.text: It applies to any meeting of the company, including an annual general meeting, wherever calling the meeting has become inconvenient
options.explanation: Two errors. Section 98 expressly excludes the annual general meeting, which is section 97's territory, and the test is IMPRACTICABILITY, not inconvenience.

options.text: It may be invoked only by a member holding not less than one-tenth of the paid-up voting capital of the company
options.explanation: No threshold applies. The Tribunal may act suo motu, and any director or any member entitled to vote may apply.

options.text: Where it is impracticable to call, hold or conduct a meeting other than an annual general meeting, the Tribunal may, suo motu or on the application of any director or of any member entitled to vote, order the meeting to be called, held and conducted as it thinks fit, and such a meeting is deemed to be duly called, held and conducted
options.explanation: Correct. That is the whole of section 98: the exclusion of the AGM, the impracticability test, the three routes to the Tribunal, and the deeming provision that validates the meeting.

options.text: A meeting ordered under section 98 requires the quorum fixed by section 103 to be present, and the Tribunal cannot dispense with it
options.explanation: The Tribunal may give ancillary directions including a direction that one member present in person or by proxy shall be deemed to constitute a meeting, which is precisely a dispensation from the ordinary quorum.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 100(2) · Requisition for an extraordinary general meeting
questions.stem: In the case of a company having a share capital, the Board is bound to call an extraordinary general meeting on a requisition made by members who, on the date of receipt of the requisition, hold not less than:

readLink.label: Read: Extraordinary general meeting — s. 100 →

options.text: One-twentieth of such of the paid-up share capital of the company as on that date carries the right of voting
options.explanation: One-twentieth is five per cent. Section 100(2)(a) sets the threshold at one-tenth.

options.text: One-tenth of such of the paid-up share capital of the company as on that date carries the right of voting
options.explanation: Correct. Note the two refinements section 100(2)(a) builds in: the measure is the paid-up capital CARRYING VOTING RIGHTS, and it is tested on the DATE OF RECEIPT of the requisition.

options.text: One-tenth of the total number of members of the company
options.explanation: The one-tenth of members test belongs to section 94(1), on where the registers may be kept. Section 100(2)(a) measures capital, not heads.

options.text: Shares on which an aggregate sum of not less than five lakh rupees has been paid up
options.explanation: The ₹5,00,000 paid-up limb appears in section 109 (demand for a poll) and section 115 (special notice), not in section 100.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 100(4) · The requisition clocks
questions.stem: A valid requisition for an extraordinary general meeting of Alaknanda Papers Limited is dated 2 June 2026 and is received at the registered office on 4 June 2026. The Board must proceed to call the meeting for a day not later than:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 100(4) — a meeting for a day not later than forty-five days from the date of receipt of the requisition

readLink.label: Read: Extraordinary general meeting — s. 100 →

options.text: 17 July 2026
options.explanation: This counts forty-five days from the DATE OF THE REQUISITION. Section 100(4) counts the forty-five days from the date of RECEIPT of the requisition.

options.text: 25 June 2026
options.explanation: That is the twenty-first day from receipt, the date by which the Board must PROCEED TO CALL the meeting. It is not the outer date for holding it.

options.text: 19 July 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Forty-five days counted from (and excluding) 4 June 2026: twenty-six days remain in June and nineteen more fall in July, giving 19 July 2026.

options.text: 2 September 2026
options.explanation: Three months from the date of the requisition is the outer limit for a meeting held by the REQUISITIONISTS themselves after the Board's default, not for the Board's own meeting.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 100(5)–(6) · A meeting held by the requisitionists
questions.stem: The Board of a company fails to act on a valid requisition and the requisitionists themselves call and hold the extraordinary general meeting. As to the expenses they reasonably incur, section 100(6) provides that:

readLink.label: Read: Extraordinary general meeting — s. 100 →

options.text: The company must reimburse the expenses, and the sums so paid are deducted from any fee or other remuneration payable to the directors who were in default in calling the meeting
options.explanation: Correct. Section 100(6) does both things: it shifts the cost to the company and then recovers it from the defaulting directors' own fee or remuneration.

options.text: The requisitionists must bear their own expenses, the statutory remedy against the Board being a penalty under section 99
options.explanation: Section 100(6) expressly provides for reimbursement. Leaving the requisitionists out of pocket would defeat the section.

options.text: The company must reimburse the expenses, and may recover them from the members generally by a call on shares
options.explanation: There is no call on members. Recovery is from the remuneration of the directors who were in default.

options.text: The Tribunal must first determine the quantum of the expenses before the company may reimburse them
options.explanation: No Tribunal order is needed. The test in the section is that the expenses be reasonable.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 101 · Twenty-one clear days and deemed service
questions.stem: Hemadri Alloys Limited posts the notice of a general meeting to its members on 1 September 2026. Service of a notice of a meeting sent by post is deemed to be effected at the expiration of forty-eight hours after the letter is posted. The earliest date on which the meeting may validly be held, without any consent to shorter notice, is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 101(1) read with rule 35(6) of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Notice and explanatory statement — ss. 101 and 102 →

options.text: 22 September 2026
options.explanation: This simply adds twenty-one days to the date of posting. It ignores both the forty-eight-hour deemed service and the requirement that the twenty-one days be CLEAR.

options.text: 23 September 2026
options.explanation: This counts twenty-one clear days from the date of POSTING. Service is deemed to occur only forty-eight hours after posting, so the count begins two days later.

options.text: 24 September 2026
options.explanation: This allows the forty-eight hours but then counts twenty-one ordinary days, not twenty-one clear days: it fails to exclude the day of the meeting.

options.text: 25 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Posted 1 September, service is deemed on 3 September. Excluding the day of service, the first clear day is 4 September and the twenty-first clear day is 24 September; excluding the day of the meeting as well, the earliest meeting date is 25 September 2026 — the shortcut is posting date plus twenty-four days.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 101(1) proviso · Consent to shorter notice
questions.stem: An annual general meeting of a company having a share capital is to be called on notice shorter than twenty-one clear days. The consent required is that of:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 101(1), first proviso, clause (i)

readLink.label: Read: Notice and explanatory statement — ss. 101 and 102 →

options.text: All the members entitled to vote at the meeting
options.explanation: Unanimity is required for the choice of an unusual PLACE for an unlisted company's AGM under section 96(2), not for shorter notice.

options.text: Members holding a majority in number of the members entitled to vote and representing not less than ninety-five per cent of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights
options.explanation: That compound test applies to a general meeting OTHER THAN an annual general meeting. For an AGM the test is simpler.

options.text: Members holding not less than three-fourths of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights
options.explanation: Three-fourths is the special-resolution ratio under section 114(2), not the shorter-notice threshold.

options.text: Not less than ninety-five per cent of the members entitled to vote at the meeting, given in writing or by electronic mode
options.explanation: Correct. Clause (i) of the first proviso to section 101(1) requires the consent of not less than ninety-five per cent of the members entitled to vote at the annual general meeting, in writing or by electronic mode.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 102(2) · Ordinary and special business
questions.stem: At an annual general meeting, which of the following items is SPECIAL business requiring an explanatory statement under section 102?

readLink.label: Read: Notice and explanatory statement — ss. 101 and 102 →

options.text: Consideration of the financial statements and the reports of the Board of Directors and the auditors
options.explanation: Expressly ordinary business under section 102(2)(a)(i).

options.text: Declaration of a dividend
options.explanation: Expressly ordinary business under section 102(2)(a)(ii).

options.text: Appointment of a managing director and approval of the terms of his appointment
options.explanation: Correct. The four items listed as ordinary business are the financial statements and reports, the dividend, directors retiring by rotation, and the auditors' appointment and remuneration. Everything else at an AGM is special business, so the appointment of a managing director needs an explanatory statement.

options.text: Appointment of directors in place of those retiring
options.explanation: Expressly ordinary business under section 102(2)(a)(iii). Note the narrowness: only directors appointed IN PLACE OF THOSE RETIRING are ordinary business.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 103 · Quorum for a general meeting
questions.stem: Sharavati Ceramics Limited is a public company. On the date of its general meeting the register of members shows 4,200 members. Its articles are silent as to quorum. The quorum for the meeting is:

readLink.label: Read: Quorum and chairman — ss. 103 and 104 →

options.text: Fifteen members personally present
options.explanation: Correct. For a public company the quorum is five members personally present where the number of members as on the date of the meeting is up to 1,000, fifteen where it is more than 1,000 but up to 5,000, and thirty where it exceeds 5,000. With 4,200 members the middle slab applies.

options.text: Five members personally present
options.explanation: Five is the quorum only where the number of members is not more than 1,000.

options.text: Thirty members personally present
options.explanation: Thirty applies only where the number of members EXCEEDS 5,000. Here there are 4,200.

options.text: Two members personally present
options.explanation: Two is the quorum for a private company. Sharavati Ceramics is a public company.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 103(2)–(3) · Absence of quorum
questions.stem: A general meeting of a public company, called by the Board, is fixed for 11 a.m. on 10 August 2026. At 11.30 a.m. the quorum is still not present. Which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Quorum and chairman — ss. 103 and 104 →

options.text: The meeting stands cancelled and a fresh notice of twenty-one clear days must be issued
options.explanation: Cancellation is the consequence only where the meeting was called by REQUISITIONISTS under section 100. A Board-called meeting is adjourned, not cancelled.

options.text: The meeting stands adjourned to the same day in the next week at the same time and place, or to such other date, time and place as the Board may determine, and if a quorum is again absent at the adjourned meeting the members present shall be the quorum
options.explanation: Correct. Section 103(2)(a) supplies the automatic adjournment and the Board's power to fix another date, time and place; section 103(3) then makes the members present the quorum at the adjourned meeting. A change of day, time or place needs at least three days' notice.

options.text: The chairman may proceed with the business, since half an hour has elapsed and the members present are deemed to be the quorum
options.explanation: The members present become the quorum only at the ADJOURNED meeting under section 103(3), never at the original meeting.

options.text: The meeting is adjourned to the same day in the next month, and the company must give not less than seven days' notice of the adjourned meeting
options.explanation: Both figures are wrong. The adjournment is to the same day in the next WEEK, and where the day, time or place is changed the notice is not less than THREE days.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 104 · Chairman of a general meeting
questions.stem: The articles of a company are silent as to who shall chair its general meetings. Under section 104, the Chairman is:

readLink.label: Read: Quorum and chairman — ss. 103 and 104 →

options.text: The chairman of the Board of Directors, who chairs general meetings by virtue of his office
options.explanation: That is a common ARTICLES provision, but the stem says the articles are silent, and section 104 then puts the choice to the members.

options.text: The managing director, or in his absence the senior-most director present
options.explanation: Section 104 confers no such office-based precedence.

options.text: A person nominated by the Board before the meeting, whose nomination the members may not question
options.explanation: The Board has no such nominating power once the articles are silent.

options.text: A member elected by the members personally present, on a show of hands; and if a poll is demanded on that election, the poll is taken forthwith and the person elected on the poll chairs the rest of the meeting
options.explanation: Correct. Section 104(1) puts the election to the members personally present on a show of hands, and section 104(2) makes the poll on that election an immediate one, the show-of-hands chairman holding office only until the poll result.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 105 · Rights and disabilities of a proxy
questions.stem: Which statement about a proxy appointed under section 105 is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 105(1), first proviso, and s. 103(1)

readLink.label: Read: Proxies and restrictions on voting — ss. 105 and 106 →

options.text: A proxy need not be a member, has no right to speak at the meeting, may vote only on a poll, and is not counted towards the quorum
options.explanation: Correct. All four propositions follow from section 105(1) and its first proviso, read with the words 'personally present' in section 105 and section 103(1). A representative appointed under section 112 or section 113 differs on every one of them.

options.text: A proxy must himself be a member of the company, and may both speak and vote at the meeting
options.explanation: Section 105(2) requires the notice to state expressly that a proxy NEED NOT be a member, and the first proviso denies him the right to speak.

options.text: A proxy may vote on a show of hands but not on a poll
options.explanation: This reverses the rule. The first proviso allows a proxy to vote only on a POLL.

options.text: A proxy is counted towards the quorum, but only in a private company
options.explanation: The quorum requires members to be personally present, and that requirement applies to private and public companies alike.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 105 · Limits on a proxy-holder and the forty-eight-hour rule
questions.stem: The articles of Tungabhadra Mills Limited require an instrument of proxy to be deposited with the company at least seventy-two hours before the meeting. Mr Iyer holds proxies for 46 members holding in the aggregate 7% of the total share capital carrying voting rights. Which statement is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 105(4), read with rule 19(2) of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules 2014 (rules-level)

readLink.label: Read: Proxies and restrictions on voting — ss. 105 and 106 →

options.text: The seventy-two-hour requirement is valid, and Mr Iyer's appointment is bad because a person may act as proxy for not more than twenty-five members
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong. Section 105(4) reads down any period longer than forty-eight hours, and the prescribed ceiling on members is fifty, not twenty-five.

options.text: The article takes effect as if it required deposit forty-eight hours before the meeting, and Mr Iyer's appointment is within the prescribed limits of not more than fifty members holding in the aggregate not more than ten per cent of the voting share capital
options.explanation: Correct. Section 105(4) converts any longer period stipulated by the articles into forty-eight hours. Mr Iyer is proxy for 46 members, which is within fifty, holding 7% in the aggregate, which is within ten per cent.

options.text: The seventy-two-hour requirement is valid because the articles may always impose stricter conditions than the Act
options.explanation: Section 105(4) is precisely a bar on stricter articles. It caps the deposit period at forty-eight hours; the articles may only shorten it.

options.text: The article is void and no deposit period may be insisted upon at all
options.explanation: The article is not void; it is read down to forty-eight hours. A company may still insist on timely deposit.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 106 · Restriction on voting rights
questions.stem: Under section 106 of the Companies Act 2013, a company may prohibit a member from exercising his voting right:

readLink.label: Read: Proxies and restrictions on voting — ss. 105 and 106 →

options.text: On any ground stated in its articles, the articles being the contract between the company and its members
options.explanation: Section 106(2) shuts this down: except on the grounds in sub-section (1), a company shall not prohibit any member from exercising his voting right on any other ground.

options.text: Where the member has failed to attend the two immediately preceding general meetings
options.explanation: Attendance is not a ground known to section 106.

options.text: Where the member has pledged his shares with a bank, until the pledge is released
options.explanation: A pledge in favour of a third party is irrelevant. The section speaks of sums payable to the COMPANY and of the company's own lien.

options.text: Only if the articles so provide, and only in respect of shares on which calls or other sums presently payable by him have not been paid, or in regard to which the company has exercised any right of lien
options.explanation: Correct. Section 106(1) permits the restriction only if the ARTICLES provide for it, and only on those two grounds; section 106(2) forbids any other ground. Section 106(3) separately allows split voting on a poll.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 107 · Voting by show of hands
questions.stem: The Chairman of a general meeting declares on a show of hands that a resolution has been carried, and an entry to that effect is made in the minutes. Under section 107(2), that declaration and entry are:

readLink.label: Read: Voting — show of hands, e-voting, poll and postal ballot — ss. 107 to 110 →

options.text: Conclusive evidence of the fact of the passing of the resolution, without proof of the number or proportion of the votes cast
options.explanation: Correct. Section 107(2) makes the Chairman's declaration together with the minute entry conclusive evidence of the fact, which is why an aggrieved member's remedy is to demand a POLL before or on the declaration of the result, under section 109.

options.text: Prima facie evidence only, rebuttable by any member who can show the actual count
options.explanation: Prima facie evidence is the standard for the registers under section 95 and for minutes under section 118(7). Section 107(2) goes further and says conclusive.

options.text: Of no evidentiary value unless the number of votes for and against is recorded in the minutes
options.explanation: The section expressly dispenses with proof of the number or proportion of the votes.

options.text: Conclusive only if a poll has also been taken and the result of the poll agrees with the show of hands
options.explanation: A poll displaces the show of hands altogether; where a poll is taken its result is deemed to be the decision of the meeting under section 109(7).

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 109 · Demand for a poll
questions.stem: Hemadri Alloys Limited has 40,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, fully paid up, each carrying one vote, and no other share capital. At a general meeting, what is the smallest number of such shares that members present in person or by proxy must hold between them to compel the Chairman to order a poll under section 109(1)(a)?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 109(1)(a) — one-tenth of the total voting power OR shares on which an aggregate of not less than ₹5,00,000 has been paid up

readLink.label: Read: Voting — show of hands, e-voting, poll and postal ballot — ss. 107 to 110 →

options.text: 4,00,000 shares
options.explanation: This applies only the first limb, one-tenth of the total voting power. The section offers an alternative limb that is satisfied by far fewer shares.

options.text: 4,50,000 shares
options.explanation: This adds the two limbs together. They are alternatives joined by 'or', never cumulative.

options.text: 50,000 shares
options.explanation: Correct. The second limb is satisfied by shares on which an aggregate of ₹5,00,000 has been paid up: at ₹10 fully paid per share that is ₹5,00,000 ÷ ₹10 = 50,000 shares. Because the limbs are alternatives, the lower requirement governs, and 50,000 is well below the 4,00,000 shares needed on the voting-power limb.

options.text: 5,00,000 shares
options.explanation: This mistakes the rupee figure of ₹5,00,000 for a number of shares. The figure is an aggregate PAID-UP AMOUNT, which must be divided by the paid-up value per share.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 110 · Postal ballot
questions.stem: Which business may NOT be transacted by means of a postal ballot under section 110?

readLink.label: Read: Voting — show of hands, e-voting, poll and postal ballot — ss. 107 to 110 →

options.text: A special resolution altering the objects clause of the memorandum
options.explanation: This is special business and may be transacted by postal ballot where the company chooses that route.

options.text: Ordinary business, and any business in respect of which directors or auditors have a right to be heard at a meeting
options.explanation: Correct. Section 110(1)(b) allows a company to use a postal ballot for any item OTHER THAN ordinary business and business on which directors or auditors have a right to be heard. Those items must go to a meeting, where the right to be heard can actually be exercised.

options.text: A resolution giving the Board consent under section 180(1)(c) to borrow beyond the paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium
options.explanation: This is special business and is capable of being transacted by postal ballot.

options.text: A resolution for the buy-back of the company's own securities
options.explanation: Again special business, and not within the exclusions in section 110(1)(b).

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 114 · Ordinary and special resolutions
questions.stem: At a general meeting the notice did not state that a particular resolution was intended to be proposed as a special resolution, but on a poll the votes cast in favour were nine times the votes cast against. The resolution is:

readLink.label: Read: Resolutions and special notice — ss. 114, 115 and 116 →

options.text: A special resolution, because the three-to-one majority in section 114(2)(c) was comfortably exceeded
options.explanation: The majority is only the third of the three conditions in section 114(2). The first condition, notice of the intention, was not satisfied.

options.text: A special resolution, because a defect in the notice is cured by the size of the majority
options.explanation: Nothing in section 114 allows a majority to cure a notice defect. The conditions are cumulative.

options.text: Invalid altogether, since a resolution passed on a defective notice is a nullity
options.explanation: The notice was not defective for an ordinary resolution; it merely failed to announce a SPECIAL resolution. The resolution survives as an ordinary one.

options.text: An ordinary resolution only, because section 114(2)(a) requires the intention to propose it as a special resolution to have been duly specified in the notice
options.explanation: Correct. A special resolution needs all three of: the intention specified in the notice, the notice required by the Act duly given, and votes in favour of not less than three times the votes against. Failing the first, what was passed is an ordinary resolution, and any action needing a special resolution cannot be taken on it.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 115 · Resolutions requiring special notice
questions.stem: Under section 115 of the Companies Act 2013, notice of the intention to move a resolution requiring special notice must be given to the company by members who hold:

readLink.label: Read: Resolutions and special notice — ss. 114, 115 and 116 →

options.text: Not less than one per cent of the total voting power, or shares on which such aggregate sum not exceeding five lakh rupees as may be prescribed has been paid up
options.explanation: Correct. Section 115 offers these two alternative limbs. Special notice is required, among other things, for a resolution under section 140(4) appointing an auditor other than the retiring auditor, and for a resolution under section 169 removing a director before the expiry of his term.

options.text: Not less than ten per cent of the total voting power, or shares on which five lakh rupees has been paid up
options.explanation: Ten per cent is the requisition threshold for an extraordinary general meeting under section 100(2) and the first limb of the poll demand under section 109. Section 115 asks for one per cent.

options.text: Not less than one-tenth in number of the members entitled to vote at the meeting
options.explanation: Section 115 measures voting power and paid-up value, never the number of members.

options.text: Not less than five per cent of the paid-up share capital of the company, irrespective of voting rights
options.explanation: Neither the percentage nor the base is right, and section 115's first limb is expressly measured on VOTING POWER.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 117 · Filing of resolutions and agreements
questions.stem: Which of the following need NOT be filed with the Registrar under section 117 of the Companies Act 2013?

readLink.label: Read: Filing of resolutions — s. 117 →

options.text: A Board resolution relating to the variation of the terms of appointment of a managing director
options.explanation: Expressly covered by section 117(3)(c), which is one of the two places where a BOARD resolution enters section 117.

options.text: A resolution according consent to the Board to exercise the power under section 180(1)(c) to borrow beyond the paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium
options.explanation: Expressly covered by section 117(3)(e), together with the section 180(1)(a) consent for the disposal of an undertaking.

options.text: An ordinary resolution declaring a dividend at the annual general meeting
options.explanation: Correct. The declaration of a dividend is ordinary business passed by an ordinary resolution and falls within no clause of section 117(3). The general rule is that ordinary resolutions are not filed unless a specific clause catches them.

options.text: A resolution agreed to by all the members which, if not so agreed, would not have been effective unless passed as a special resolution
options.explanation: Expressly covered by section 117(3)(b). Unanimity does not remove the filing obligation.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 118 and 119 · Minutes and their inspection
questions.stem: Which statement about minutes under sections 118 and 119 is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Minutes, inspection and electronic records — ss. 118, 119 and 120 →

options.text: Minutes must be prepared and signed within fifteen days of the conclusion of the meeting, and a member may inspect the minutes of both general meetings and Board meetings
options.explanation: Two errors. The period is thirty days, and section 119 opens only the minutes of GENERAL MEETINGS and of postal-ballot resolutions to members.

options.text: Minutes of every general meeting, of every meeting of a class of shareholders or creditors, of every postal-ballot resolution and of every Board and committee meeting must be prepared, signed and kept within thirty days of the conclusion of the meeting, in books with consecutively numbered pages; and the company must observe the secretarial standards on general and Board meetings
options.explanation: Correct. That is section 118(1) read with section 118(10), which makes SS-1 for Board meetings and SS-2 for general meetings mandatory. The pages must be consecutively numbered, and tampering with the minutes attracts imprisonment under section 118(12).

options.text: The Chairman must include in the minutes every matter raised at the meeting, and has no discretion to exclude anything
options.explanation: Section 118(5) and (6) give the Chairman ABSOLUTE DISCRETION to exclude matter that is defamatory, irrelevant or immaterial, or detrimental to the interests of the company.

options.text: A member is entitled to a copy of the minutes of a general meeting within seven days of his request, free of charge
options.explanation: Section 119(2) allows SEVEN WORKING DAYS and permits the company to charge the prescribed fee. Contrast section 94(3), where a copy of a register must be furnished within seven days.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 89 and 90 · Beneficial interest and significant beneficial owners
questions.stem: Explain the declarations required under section 89 of the Companies Act 2013 where the registered holder of shares is not the person holding the beneficial interest in them, and outline the obligations that section 90 imposes in relation to a significant beneficial owner, including the company's remedy where a person fails to respond to the company's notice. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 89(1): a person whose name is entered in the register of members of a company as the holder of shares but who does not hold the beneficial interest in them must make a declaration to the company, in the prescribed form, within thirty days of his name being entered in the register, specifying the name and particulars of the person who holds the beneficial interest

Section 89(2) and (3): every person who holds or acquires a beneficial interest in a share but is not the registered holder must likewise declare to the company within thirty days of acquiring the beneficial interest, giving the particulars of the registered holder; and where there is any change in the beneficial interest, both persons must make a further declaration within thirty days of the change

Section 89(6) and (8): where a declaration is received, the company must file a return with the Registrar within thirty days of receipt, in the prescribed form and with the prescribed fee; and where a required declaration is not made, no right in relation to the share is enforceable by the person holding the beneficial interest — but this does not relieve the company of its obligation to pay dividend to the registered owner

Section 90(1) and (2): every INDIVIDUAL who, acting alone or together, or through one or more persons or a trust (including a trust and persons resident outside India), holds beneficial interests of not less than twenty-five per cent, or such other percentage as may be prescribed (presently ten per cent under the Significant Beneficial Owners Rules), or who has the right to exercise significant influence or control, must declare his interest to the company; the company must maintain a register of significant beneficial owners, open to members' inspection on payment of the prescribed fee, and file a return with the Registrar
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 90(1), (2), (4) with the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules 2018

skeleton.point: Section 90(5) to (9): the company must give notice to any person it knows or has reason to believe to be a significant beneficial owner; the person must reply within thirty days; on failure to give the information or where the company is not satisfied with the reply, the company must apply to the TRIBUNAL within fifteen days of the expiry of that period for an order restricting the shares — restriction on transfer of interest, suspension of voting rights, suspension of the right to receive dividend or any other restriction; the Tribunal decides within sixty days after hearing the parties, and where no application for relaxation is made within one year of the order the shares are transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 92 · Annual return
questions.stem: State the particulars that the annual return of a company must contain under section 92(1) of the Companies Act 2013, explain who must sign it and when it must be certified by a company secretary in practice, and state the time limit for filing it with the Registrar. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 92(1): the annual return contains the particulars as they stood on the close of the financial year regarding the registered office, principal business activities and particulars of holding, subsidiary and associate companies; shares, debentures and other securities and the shareholding pattern; members and debenture-holders with changes since the close of the previous financial year; promoters, directors and key managerial personnel with changes; meetings of members or a class of them and of the Board and its committees with attendance details; remuneration of directors and key managerial personnel; penalties imposed on the company, its directors or officers and details of compounding of offences and appeals; matters relating to certification of compliances and disclosures as prescribed; and such other matters as may be prescribed

Note for the answer: the clauses formerly requiring the company's INDEBTEDNESS and the details of shares held by or on behalf of foreign institutional investors were omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2017 and must not be listed
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 92(1) — clauses omitted by Act 1 of 2018

skeleton.point: Signing (first and third provisos to s. 92(1)): the return is signed by a director AND the company secretary, or where there is no company secretary, by a company secretary in practice; in the case of a One Person Company and a small company, it is signed by the company secretary, or where there is no company secretary, by the director of the company
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 92(1), first and third provisos

skeleton.point: Certification (second proviso to s. 92(1)): the annual return of a LISTED company, or of a company having paid-up share capital of ten crore rupees or more OR turnover of fifty crore rupees or more, must also be certified by a company secretary in practice, in the prescribed form, to the effect that the return discloses the facts correctly and adequately and that the company has complied with all the provisions of the Act; the thresholds are prescribed by rule and are amendment-sensitive
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 92(1), second proviso, with rule 11(2) of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules 2014

skeleton.point: Section 92(3): every company must place a copy of the annual return on its website, if any, and the web link must be disclosed in the Board's report

Section 92(4): the return must be filed with the Registrar within sixty days from the date on which the annual general meeting is held, or, where no annual general meeting is held in any year, within sixty days from the date on which the annual general meeting SHOULD have been held, together with a statement specifying the reasons for not holding it

Section 92(5) and (6): default by the company attracts a penalty on the company and every officer in default with a continuing daily component and a cap; and a company secretary in practice who certifies the return otherwise than in conformity with the requirements of the section and the rules is separately liable to a penalty

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 96 · Annual general meeting
questions.stem: Vaitarna Engineering Limited was incorporated on 12 June 2024 and closed its first financial year on 31 March 2025. It held its first annual general meeting on 20 December 2025. Advise the company on the last date by which it must hold its next annual general meeting for the financial year ended 31 March 2026, and state the provisions of section 96 of the Companies Act 2013 governing the time, extension of time, and the day, hour and place of an annual general meeting. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 96(1), first proviso, first limb: the FIRST annual general meeting must be held within nine months from the date of closing of the first financial year; applied here, nine months from 31 March 2025 expired on 31 December 2025, so the meeting held on 20 December 2025 was in time, and no annual general meeting was required in the year of incorporation
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 96(1), first and second provisos

skeleton.point: Section 96(1), first proviso, second limb: every other annual general meeting must be held within six months from the date of closing of the financial year; six months from 31 March 2026 expires on 30 September 2026

Section 96(1), main limb: not more than fifteen months may elapse between the date of one annual general meeting and that of the next; fifteen months from 20 December 2025 expires on 20 March 2027. Both limits operate together and the EARLIER date governs, so the next annual general meeting must be held on or before 30 SEPTEMBER 2026

Section 96(1), third proviso: the Registrar may, for any special reason, extend the time within which any annual general meeting, OTHER THAN THE FIRST, shall be held, by a period not exceeding three months; so on a special reason shown the deadline here could be extended to 30 December 2026, but the first annual general meeting can never be extended

Section 96(2): every annual general meeting must be called during business hours, that is between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m., on a day that is not a National Holiday declared as such by the Central Government, and must be held either at the registered office or at some other place within the city, town or village in which the registered office is situate; an unlisted company may hold it at any place in India if consent is given in writing or in electronic mode by all the members in advance. Default in holding the meeting exposes the company to an application by any member to the Tribunal under s. 97 and to punishment under s. 99
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 96(2) with ss. 97 and 99

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 100 and 101 · Requisitioned EGM and notice of a general meeting
questions.stem: Explain the circumstances in which the Board of a company is bound to call an extraordinary general meeting on the requisition of its members, the consequences of the Board's failure to do so, and the requirements as to notice of a general meeting under section 101 of the Companies Act 2013. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 100(1): the Board may call an extraordinary general meeting whenever it deems fit; the proviso requires such a meeting to be held at a place within India, except in the case of a company that is a wholly owned subsidiary of a company incorporated outside India

Section 100(2): the Board SHALL call an extraordinary general meeting on a requisition made, in the case of a company having a share capital, by members holding on the date of receipt of the requisition not less than one-tenth of such of the paid-up share capital as carries the right of voting; and, in the case of a company not having a share capital, by members having not less than one-tenth of the total voting power of all the members having a right to vote on that date

Section 100(3): the requisition must set out the matters for the consideration of which the meeting is to be called, be signed by the requisitionists, and be sent to the registered office of the company

Section 100(4): if the Board does not, within twenty-one days from the date of receipt of a valid requisition, proceed to call a meeting for a day not later than forty-five days from the date of receipt of the requisition, the meeting may be called and held by the requisitionists themselves within a period of three months from the date of the requisition — note the different starting points: receipt for the twenty-one and forty-five days, the date of the requisition for the three months

Section 100(5) and (6): a meeting called by the requisitionists must be called and held in the same manner in which a meeting is called and held by the Board; and any reasonable expenses incurred by the requisitionists must be reimbursed by the company, the sums so paid being deducted from any fee or other remuneration payable to the directors who were in default in calling the meeting

Section 101(1): a general meeting may be called by giving not less than CLEAR twenty-one days' notice, in writing or through electronic mode; 'clear' excludes both the day on which the notice is served and the day of the meeting, and where the notice is sent by post service is deemed to be effected at the expiration of forty-eight hours after posting
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 101(1) with rule 35(6) of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules 2014

skeleton.point: Section 101(1) proviso and s. 101(2) to (4): shorter notice is permitted with consent in writing or by electronic mode of not less than ninety-five per cent of the members entitled to vote at an annual general meeting, and, for any other general meeting of a company having a share capital, of members holding a majority in number of those entitled to vote and representing not less than ninety-five per cent of the paid-up share capital giving a right to vote; the notice must state the place, date, day and hour and the business to be transacted, must be given to every member, to the auditors and to every director, and an accidental omission to give notice or the non-receipt of notice does not invalidate the proceedings
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 101(1) proviso and s. 101(2), (3) and (4)

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 103 and 105 · Quorum and proxies
questions.stem: State the quorum for a general meeting under section 103 of the Companies Act 2013 and the consequences where a quorum is not present, and explain the rights and disabilities of a proxy appointed under section 105. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 103(1): unless the articles provide for a larger number, the quorum for a public company is five members personally present where the number of members as on the date of the meeting is not more than one thousand, fifteen members personally present where it is more than one thousand but up to five thousand, and thirty members personally present where it exceeds five thousand; for a private company the quorum is two members personally present

The words 'personally present' exclude a proxy, who is therefore not counted towards the quorum; but a representative appointed by a body corporate under section 113, and a representative of the President of India or a Governor appointed under section 112, are treated as members personally present and ARE counted
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 103(1) with ss. 112 and 113

skeleton.point: Section 103(2): if a quorum is not present within half an hour from the time appointed, the meeting stands adjourned to the same day in the next week at the same time and place, or to such other date, time and place as the Board may determine; but a meeting called on the requisition of members under section 100 stands CANCELLED. Where the meeting is adjourned or the day, time or place is changed, the company must give not less than three days' notice to the members individually or by advertisement in two newspapers, one in English and one in the vernacular language, in circulation at the place of the registered office
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 103(2) and its proviso

skeleton.point: Section 103(3): if at the adjourned meeting also a quorum is not present within half an hour, the members present shall be the quorum. Section 105: any member entitled to attend and vote may appoint a proxy, who need not be a member; but a proxy has NO right to speak at the meeting and is entitled to vote only on a POLL; an article requiring the proxy instrument to be deposited more than forty-eight hours before the meeting takes effect as if it required forty-eight hours; and at rules level one person may act as proxy for not more than fifty members holding in the aggregate not more than ten per cent of the total share capital carrying voting rights
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 103(3) and s. 105(1), (2) and (4) with rule 19(2) of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules 2014

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 118, 119, 121 and 122 · Minutes, inspection, AGM report and OPC
questions.stem: Explain the requirements of the Companies Act 2013 as to the preparation, signing and evidentiary value of minutes of meetings, the right of a member to inspect them, the report on the annual general meeting of a listed public company, and the modifications made by section 122 for a One Person Company. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 118(1) to (3): every company must cause minutes of the proceedings of every general meeting, of every meeting of a class of shareholders or creditors, of every resolution passed by postal ballot, and of every meeting of the Board or a committee of the Board, to be prepared and signed in the prescribed manner and kept WITHIN THIRTY DAYS of the conclusion of the meeting or the passing of the resolution, in books kept for that purpose with their pages consecutively numbered; the minutes must contain a fair and correct summary of the proceedings, and all appointments made at the meeting must be included

Section 118(4) to (6): minutes of a Board or committee meeting must also record the names of the directors present and, for each resolution, the names of the directors dissenting from or not concurring with it; nothing may be included that in the opinion of the Chairman is or could reasonably be regarded as defamatory of any person, or is irrelevant or immaterial to the proceedings, or is detrimental to the interests of the company, and the Chairman has ABSOLUTE DISCRETION on inclusion or exclusion on those grounds

Section 118(7), (8), (10) and (12): minutes kept in accordance with the section are evidence of the proceedings recorded, and until the contrary is proved the meeting is deemed to have been duly called and held, the proceedings to have duly taken place and all appointments of directors, key managerial personnel, auditors and a company secretary in practice to be valid; every company must observe the secretarial standards on general and Board meetings specified by the Institute of Company Secretaries of India and approved by the Central Government; and tampering with the minutes is punishable with imprisonment and a fine

Section 119: the books containing the minutes of GENERAL MEETINGS and of resolutions passed by postal ballot must be kept at the registered office and be open during business hours to inspection by any member without charge, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by the articles or in general meeting so that not less than two hours in each business day are allowed; a member is entitled to a copy within seven working days of his request on payment of the prescribed fee; refusal attracts a penalty for each refusal, and the Tribunal may order immediate inspection or direct that the copy be sent forthwith. Minutes of BOARD meetings are not open to members

Section 121: every listed public company must prepare a report on each annual general meeting, in the prescribed manner, including a confirmation that the meeting was convened, held and conducted as per the Act and the rules, and must file a copy with the Registrar within thirty days of the conclusion of the annual general meeting; default attracts penalties on the company and every officer in default. Section 122: section 98 and sections 100 to 111 do not apply to a One Person Company, and any business required to be transacted at a general meeting or, where there is only one director, at a Board meeting, is validly done where the resolution is communicated by the member (or made by the sole director) and entered in the minutes book, signed and dated, that date being deemed to be the date of the meeting for all purposes of the Act

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Case: AGM deadlines, extension, annual return and the AGM report
questions.case: Nilgiri Beverages Limited is a listed public company whose financial year closes on 31 March. Its annual general meeting for the year ended 31 March 2025 was held on 20 September 2025. For the year ended 31 March 2026 the Board is unable to finalise the accounts in time and applies to the Registrar, showing a special reason, for the maximum extension the law allows. The Registrar grants it. The annual general meeting is eventually convened and held, and concludes, on 15 December 2026.

readLink.label: Read: Annual general meeting — s. 96 →

questions.stem: Taking account of the maximum extension the Registrar may grant, the last date by which Nilgiri Beverages Limited could lawfully hold its annual general meeting for the year ended 31 March 2026 is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 96(1) and its third proviso

options.text: 30 December 2026
options.explanation: Correct. The unextended due date is the earlier of six months from 31 March 2026, which is 30 September 2026, and fifteen months from 20 September 2025, which is 20 December 2026 — that is, 30 September 2026. The Registrar may extend that date by not more than three months, giving 30 December 2026.

options.text: 31 December 2026
options.explanation: This treats the extension as running to the calendar year-end. The three months are counted from the due date of 30 September 2026, which lands on 30 December 2026.

options.text: 20 March 2027
options.explanation: This extends the fifteen-month gap by a further three months. The extension operates on the DUE DATE for holding the meeting, and in any event the due date was fixed by the six-month limb, not the gap limb.

options.text: 30 September 2026
options.explanation: That is the unextended due date. The stem asks for the date after the maximum extension the Registrar may grant.

questions.stem: The annual general meeting having been held and concluded on 15 December 2026, the last date for filing the company's annual return with the Registrar under section 92(4) is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 92(4) — sixty days from the date on which the AGM is held

options.text: 14 January 2027
options.explanation: This allows thirty days. Thirty days is the clock for filing resolutions under section 117 and the AGM report under section 121; the annual return has sixty days.

options.text: 13 February 2027
options.explanation: Correct. Sixty days counted from (and excluding) 15 December 2026: sixteen days remain in December, thirty-one fall in January, and thirteen more give 13 February 2027.

options.text: 15 February 2027
options.explanation: This reads sixty days as two calendar months. December and January together have sixty-two days, so the calendar-month reading lands two days late.
